title: A combined shading and radiation simulation tool for defining agrivoltaic systems
abstract: Agrivoltaic systems have the potential to resolve rapidly rising global food and energy challenges by co-locating agriculture and solar photovoltaics (PV). In the United States, Massachusetts created the Solar Massachusetts Renewable Target (SMART) Program to incentivize agrivoltaic development. The program relies on a shading-only simulation tool to differentiate agrivoltaic sites from traditional solar farms. In this paper, we demonstrate that radiation must be considered along with shading to identify land suitable for agricultural activity in agrivoltaic systems. To this end, we present a combined shading and radiation simulation tool and show that percent shade does not singularly determine land available for crop growth. Thus, we recommend the SMART Program update their current method for defining agrivoltaic systems to include radiation modeling.

## An observational study on the microclimate and soil thermal regimes under solar photovoltaic arrays

## Junqing Zheng[a][,][b] , Yong Luo[a][,][b][,][*] , Rui Chang[c] , Xiaoqing Gao[d ]

## A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T

> _Keywords:_ The high demand for low-carbon energy sources to mitigate climate change has prompted a rapid increase in

> Large-scale photovoltaics ground-mounted solar parks. The implementation of photovoltaic (PV) significantly impacted the local climate

> Microclimate characteristics and ecosystem, which are both poorly understood. To investigate the effects of a typical solar park on the Gobi Soil characteristics Gobi area ecological system, local microclimate and soil thermal regimes were measured year-round under and between PV arrays, at an applied solar park sited in Xinjiang, China. Our results demonstrated their seasonal and diurnal Surface energy balance changes. Under solar PV arrays, the mean annual net radiation and wind speed decreased by 92.68 % and 50.53 % respectively. In contrast, PV panels caused an increase of the rear sides air by 10.12 % with 0.87[◦] C. Southfacing PV panels reduced wind speed with the prevailing northerly wind below. In addition, the relative humidity rapidly decreased when snow covered the ground, but slightly increased from April to September. We found the soil under PV panels was cooler and tended to be a sink of energy during spring and summer whereas was more often a source during autumn and winter compared with the soil between PV panels. Observed data developed the understanding of the energy processes of solar parks in Gobi ecosystems and provided evidence to support the sustainable management of the solar park.

## **1. Introduction**

Major transitions in the energy sector have been required since the rapid depletion of the global reserves of conventional energy sources in recent years [15]. Besides, conventional energy sources are harmful to the environment and aggravate global warming. For global sustainable development, the utilization of renewable energy resources is considered as a solution to replace non-renewable energy in the future [29]. As one of the reliable and sustainable energies, solar energy plays an essential role in sustainable development strategies all over the world, and the installation of photovoltaic (PV) facilities is an effective way to use solar energy. Currently, actions for renewable supply have been implemented in many countries [14], with the total global installed capacity of solar power had reached 843 GW by 2022 [16]. Following the UN’s sustainable development goals, actions against climate change through sustainable energy will continue around the world. According to the report of the International Energy Agency [13], in order to

achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, solar PV and wind generation will account for 68 % of global total electricity generation. In China, objectives of accelerating the development of renewable energy are proposed in nine clean energy bases [33], including northwest China, which is a particularly ideal location for the development of solar energy due to its high solar potential [5] and abundant land resources. However, covering the surface with sunlight-absorbing panels may impact the ‘local climate’ [3], and it will not be ignored as the vigorous expansion of the PV power stations.

In recent years, the climatic impact of PV has received worldwide considerable attention. For instance, field studies in North America observed warmer air temperatures at the PV station [8,2], and the observation studies in Qinghai province [9,34], Gansu province [35,4], Inner Mongolia province [37], and Xinjiang province [17] of China also revealed the air temperature in PV farm was warmer. However, it was notable that the warmer impact on air temperature was obvious in daytime or summer, and in some regions, the nighttime air temperature

might decrease (Wu et al., 2021). Based on a solar park sited on a grassland in the UK, Armstrong et al. [1] studied the air temperature under the PV panels and found lower air temperature, and this change was consistent with the calculated land surface temperature under the PV arrays in Qinghai province of China [3]. Uncertainty about the results may be attributed to different observation conditions. Except for the changed air temperature, some research also focused on local surface radiation balance. Apparent variations of the surface shortwave and longwave radiation components occurred throughout the whole year due to the interception of the PV panels and the reflection of the surface [34,3,21]. Tang et al. [30] captured a wind flow under the interference of a solar PV array in a desert and verified the reduction of wind velocity, as reported by Armstrong et al. [1] and Jiang et al. [17], and the direction of the airflow was strongly influenced at the same time. The air relative humidity in the PV farm showed an increased tendency according to the field studies in Qinghai province [9,32], however, under the PV arrays, absolute humidity varied with time and season [1]. Regarding the impacts of PV panels on the soil, only a few studies have been performed based on observation. Studies located in different regions worldwide showed the shading of PV panels resulted in a decrease in soil temperature [27,1,10,25], even though PV shading conditions were different [36]. The soil heat flux played an important role in calculating local energy flux [38,22]. Based on the observational data, the soil heat flux in the PV farm had been discussed in previous research, which suggested that PV plants reduced the storage of soil heat [2].

Earlier studies have shown the microclimate and soil thermal regimes difference inside and outside the PV farms without under the PV arrays (Barron-Gafford et al. 2016; [2], or ignore the soil thermal regimes under PV arrays [1], or pay no attention to near-surface climate [32]. Although previous studies provided observational data on PV farms worldwide, there was still a lack of field observation focus on both climate and soil thermal regimes under PV panels in the Gobi Desert. Efficiently utilized PV systems, including bifacial PV technology for high-energy yield [11], agrivoltaics systems for land use intensification [18], ecovoltaics systems for biodiversity preservation and ecological conservation [12], are seriously considered to ensure sustainable deployment in recent years, showed an urgent need for the microclimate data under PV panels. Meanwhile, microclimates are known to influence local soil and its relationship with plants, further affecting vegetation composition and productivity. For example, despite the sun-shading issue, the integration of herbal plants under solar PV panels showed good growth progress [26], while the plant diversity and above-ground biomass of a meadow solar park showed a decreasing trend [1].

Currently, both the climate and ecosystem impact of PV implementation are poorly understood. As the increase of the market share of bifacial PV, as well as the expansion of PV in Arid and semiarid regions with fragile and sensitive ecological environments [31], it is essential to conduct more field observations under PV panels about climate and ecosystem, to figure out the mechanisms and interactions of the impacts. Reliable suggestions will be given for fighting desertification and achieving sustainable development with the unused space under PV arrays based on this study.

In this study, we observed the varying microclimate and soil thermal regimes under solar PV arrays in a Gobi ecosystem located in Xinjiang, China, where described as an “Arid zone cold steppe” through Koppen  ̈ climate classification [20]. By comparing the results with the gap area between PV panels, this research aims to answer the following questions: 1) How do PV panels influence the Gobi microclimate and soil thermal regimes under PV panels on diurnal and seasonal scales? 2) How to efficiently utilize PV systems based on the induced microclimate and soil characteristics? Our research provided additional insight into the climatic effects of PV panels, and further had a good reference value for intermingling utilizing solar panels with other systems for sustainable development.

## **2. Materials and methods**

## _2.1. Site description_

This research was conducted at Xuyang Solar Park, China (44[◦] 24′23′′N and 87[◦] 39′23′′E; 439 m above sea level; 190 mm mean annual precipitation; 175 mm mean annual snow depth), a 70 MW capacity solar park located at Wujiaqu of Xinjiang Province, which was installed in 2015. The PV array rows were 2.4 m wide, had a gap between the rows of 7 m, faced south, and were at an angle of 30[◦] . The ground clearance of the PVs was 2.3 m. Prior to conversion to a solar park, the field site was the Gobi with sparse vegetation. The site was mowed with ~1.2 m wide strips in front of the PV arrays annually to prevent shading to the PV arrays. To determine the effects of the solar PV arrays on microclimate, measurements were made in two plots: under the PV arrays and in the gap between the PV arrays. Each plot was close to the center of the solar park. Fig. 1 shows the photos of the two monitoring plots in the PV Solar Park. The climatic and ecological impacts of PV panels were inferred from the differences between the two plots.

## _2.2. Monitoring equipment & variables_

Air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, wind direction, and four-component radiation (downward and upward shortwave radiation, downward and upward longwave radiation) were monitored above the surface at 1 m and 2 m under and between the PV arrays respectively. An air temperature and humidity sensor (HC2S3, Campbell) and a twodimensional ultrasonic anemometer (WINDSONIC, Gill) were mounted at the gap between the PV arrays, and a compact weather station (GMX600, Gill) was mounted under the PV arrays. A white fourcomponent radiation sensor (CNR 4, Kipp&Zonen) was mounted on both plots. Four 110PV thermistors (110PV, Campbell) were adhered to the back of a solar panel to measure the temperature of the PV module surface. In addition, soil temperature (5 cm depth below the surface) was measured using a hydra probe sensor (Hydra Probe II, Stevens), and soil heat flux (5 cm and 20 cm depth below the surface) was measured using soil heat flux sensors (HFP01, Campbell). At each plot, microclimate and soil thermal regimes metrics were sampled every minute, and the average over every 10 min was recorded from 01/10/21 00:00 to 30/09/22 23:50, to characterize the seasonal variation (spring is from March to May, summer is from June to August, autumn is from September to November, winter is from December to February) of the climate and soil thermal regimes associated with daytime and nighttime. The time system used in this paper is the Beijing time (BJT, UTC + 8).

**Fig. 1.** Photos of the monitoring plots under the PV arrays (a) and the reference site at the midpoint of two rows of PV arrays (b) in the solar park.

## _2.3. Data processing_

Statistical analysis was performed on the processed observational data to contrast the measured variations under the PV arrays and in the gap between the PV arrays. All statistics were undertaken using MATLAB. Observed microclimate and soil thermal regime parameters between two plots were tested for significance using a Wilcoxon rank sum test and p values _<_ 0.05 were deemed significant. Because the bad weather from 05/01/21 00:00 BJT to 19/01/21 23:50 BJT caused instrument failure, all the data during this period were marked as NaN values. Additionally, obvious and unreasonable outlier data were removed. For example, the wind speed observations exceeding 20 m/s between the PV arrays and exceeding 10 m/s under the PV arrays were removed. Downward shortwave radiation less than zero during daytime and exceeding zero during nighttime was corrected to zero. Removed data were replaced by the mean value of the last and next 10 min. To be detailed, 0.26 %, 0.25 %, 1.31 %, 0.24 %, 46.42 %, 2.43 %, 0.25 %, and 0.25 % outlier data were removed respectively for air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, wind direction, and downward shortwave radiation (RDS), upward shortwave radiation (RUS), downward longwave radiation (RDL), and upward longwave radiation (RUL) between PV arrays. Under PV arrays, these removed data account for 8.41 %, 0.29 %, 0.32 %, 0.28 %, 46.35 %, 9.60 %, 0.29 %, and 0.29 % of the observed data respectively. The net radiation (Rn) can be calculated by RDS, RUS, RDL, and RUL:

All data used in this paper were produced every 10 min and were used to compute the daytime and nighttime means during each month. Considering the intensity of solar radiation varied throughout the year, the daytime for each month was defined according to the measured seasonal RDS at Xuyang Solar Park (Table 1).

## **3. Results**

The effect of PV panels on microclimate varied seasonally and diurnally. In the following sections, we outlined the measured variation in microclimate and soil thermal regimes within the solar park. In consideration of solar radiation played an important role in PV technology, it will be analyzed in a single section. In order to clarify the mechanisms of the increased air temperature, we further analyzed the temperature of the PV module. Because the working time of a PV power station is during the daytime, we further investigated the daytime and nighttime microclimate and soil characteristics according to the measured mean monthly RDS (Table 1). We found significant differences (p _<_ 0.05) in all measured variations between the two plots.

From May to August, RUL was higher while RDL was lower under PV panels, which was supported by the higher air temperature on the rear side and lower temperature on the land surface respectively.

## _3.2. The effect of PV arrays on the local microclimate_

There were clear differences in the microclimate due to the presence of the PV panels at both seasonal and diurnal scales. Fig. 3 demonstrates the temporal variation of the microclimate under the PV arrays and in the gap between the PV arrays. Compared to the gap plot, PV panels cause an annual average Rn decrease of 193.98 W/m[2 ] (Fig. 3a), wind speed decrease of 0.69 m/s (Fig. 3c), air temperature increase of 0.87[◦] C (Fig. 3e), and relative humidity decrease of 2.22 % (Fig. 3g). The installation of PV panels decreased the mean annual Rn and wind speed by 92.68 % and 50.53 % respectively, but increased rear side air temperature by 10.12 %.

The diurnal cycle of Rn under PV panels was generally lower than that in the gap area. Compared to the gap plot, the annual mean Rn and 18.87 under PV panels was significantly lower with 319.69 W/m[2 ] W/m[2 ] for the daytime and nighttime respectively. The daytime average Rn for each season has decreased by over 94 % except for winter (by 84.64 %). The Rn between PV arrays was maximum at 14:00–15:00 BJT depending on the season. However, because of the change in solar elevation angle, the maximum Rn under the PV panels occurred in the period of time after sunrise and before sunset except for winter (Fig. 3b). Rn showed peaks at approximately 12:30 BJT during the daytime which were generated by the space between PV panels above the supporting frame.

Wind speed was greatest in summer and lowest in winter, and there was a significant change in two plots. The impact of the PV arrays on air turbulence was shown by the decrease in wind speed. Notably slower wind speeds occurred throughout the diurnal cycle over the observational period under PV panels (Fig. 3d). ## **4. Discussions**

Recently, more and more researchers paid attention to the climate and ecosystem impact of the installation of PV panels. Most of them revealed how a PV plant affects the micro-climate in surrounding areas by comparing the climate inside and outside large-scale PV farms. The result showed that the installation of the PV farm increased local daytime air temperature [8,2], decreased wind speed, and changed wind direction [17,30], increased relative humidity [35,32], and decreased annual net radiation [21]. Nevertheless, what will the climate and soil be under PV panels are rarely mentioned. Based on one-year observations, a typical Gobi solar park in northwest China was characterized by lower Rn and wind speed under PV panels, along with higher rear side air temperatures, as a result of the installation of PV panels. The change in relative humidity was associated with snow cover time, which revealed that PV panels were also a barrier to evaporation (Fig. 2g).

In the following sections, we discussed the shading and buffer effects of the PV arrays by the measured microclimate and soil thermal regimes data under PV panels. We further discussed the existing efficient PV utilization technologies under PV panels for supporting the strategic decision that aims for sustainable development. In addition, the limitations of our research are listed.

## _4.1. The shading and buffer effect of PV panels_

The shading effect of PV panels is composed of the shade of the radiation transfer and heat flux transfer, causing the change of radiation and temperature. Since a great mass of shortwave radiation was converted by the PV module to electricity during the daytime, the shading

The result showed that the temperature of the PV module was much higher than the ambient temperature by 12.39[◦] C during the daytime and lower by 2.82[◦] C during the night. The increase of air temperature under PV arrays during daytime was strongly related to the temperature of the PV module (Fig. 6). A linear relationship (R[2 ] = 0.98) between PV module temperature and ambient temperature in this study (Fig. 5) was the same as previous study [28]. The physical shading by PV arrays reduces the heat absorption of the soils during the spring and summer and prevents soil from heat loss during autumn and winter. A cooler near-surface air temperature was also observed in a UK solar park [1]. The physical shading also switched the direction of the airflow under PV panels, leading to an incline to the lower edge, which was similar to the field observations of Tang et al. (2016).

A rather agreement in the buffer effects of the PV panels on soil thermal regimes occurs over a year on different soil depths (Fig. 8). The PV array deployments removed the energy in the form of electrical energy during the day, which strongly influenced the heat absorption of the soils and significantly slower the response of soil thermal regimes to air temperature. The noticeable buffer effects are shown in Fig. 8. A much lower day-to-day variability with related changes was manifested in the soil under PV panels except in winter, showing the buffer effect of the PV panels. In winter, the buffer effect was limited especially in the topsoil, which was apparently associated with the snow cover between the PV panels. In addition, Fig. 3 showed a significant decrease in the standard deviation of the wind speed, indicating the buffer effect on the near-surface airflow.

## _4.2. Efficient utilization of PV technologies_

The efficient utilization of PV systems has received much attention in recent years. For example, bifacial solar PV collects photons simultaneously from both its front and rear sides [24], which targets to use solar resources efficiently by improving the energy output of PV systems. For intensifying land use, agrivoltaics systems and ecovoltaics systems have been tested recently around the world, aiming for at least equivalent production and biomass to that of an open-field crop and plant [12,18,7]. Moreover, roof-mounted PV and floating PV are developed to efficiently use the large surface area and underutilized space under PV arrays [6,39]. Thus, observations under PV arrays were requested to support the sustainable management of these emerging technologies.

Our research provided good reference value for intermingling utilizing solar panels with other systems for sustainable development. For instance, the bifacial PV system, which has higher performance in generating electricity, may have the potential of producing additional power of 7 % over mono facial panels during a year, and showed more efficiency in winter with an increase of 13 % in Wujiaqu. Moreover, although the growing season (summer) daytime RDL decreased by a mean of 50.75 W/m2, RUL increased by a mean of 81.15 W/m2. Since plants will receive the most energy as longwave radiation in shaded conditions [19], they may maintain good growth progress in agrivoltaics systems in Xinjiang [26,18]. Besides, noticeably higher relative humidity during daytime under PV panels can strongly reduce evapotranspiration losses, which may reduce plant drought stress [23]. The benefit of PV panels in windbreak and sand fixation is supported by our results of decreasing wind speed under PV arrays, which was also shown by Tang et al. [30].

## _4.3. Limitation_

A primary limitation in this study is the instrument accuracy, but it is unavoidable in worldwide observational studies [2]. In future studies, the observation period should try to be longer with less inaccuracy data, and the failed observations in winter should be avoided. Additionally, the observation heights were different between the two plots under the restrictions of the PV arrays, which should be identical in further parallel

observations.

As for the design of the observational experiment, there are three main limitations. First, there is a need to conduct substantially same measurement near the edge of the solar park, since the results may show differences in different areas, especially in wind direction [17]. Second, more measurements should be conducted for other suitable locations. Our results are extendable to other locations with a similar climate and ground condition based on the partly similar exchange process of radiation, water, and heat, but are not extendable outside the Gobi Desert. Third, our study neglected some constructive factors for a PV farm, such as ground coverage ratio, height and angle of the PV arrays, as well as type of PV mounting (i.e. trackers, fixed tilt, or bifacial), which are critical for near-surface climate and soil. As a result, comparison based on different constructive factors may be necessary for later relative studies.

## **5. Conclusion**

Our results show, for the first time, the seasonal and diurnal variation in microclimate and soil thermal regimes under PV panels based on parallel observations from two plots in one solar farm for a particular location in the China Gobi Desert. We further summarized the shading and buffer effects of the PV panels. In the end, we empirically discussed the reasonability of existing efficient utilization types of PV technology based on the observation results.

The implementation of PV directly influences the microclimate and soil, and how they will change is critical. Given the quantifiable differences in the microclimate here, the innovative contribution in this study presented that the installation of PV panels decreased the mean annual net radiation and wind speed by 92.68 % and 50.53 % respectively but increased rear side air temperature by 10.12 % with 0.87[◦] C. Southfacing PV panels decreased wind speed notably with prevailing north wind below. The relative humidity rapidly decreased when snow covered the ground, but slightly increased from April to September. The soil under PV panels was cooler throughout the year, and tended to be a sink of energy during spring and summer whereas was more often a source during autumn and winter compared with the soil between PV panels.

Our observed data quantified the impact of PV panels on microclimates and soil in the Gobi area, where is considered one of the most potential regions for solar energy development in China. However, because of the long-lasting snow cover and sparse vegetation in the solar park, the findings presented here may be specific to the Gobi of Xinjiang. Besides, the instrument failure during winter caused an overestimation of the annual temperature. Consequently, further long-term, continuous, and cumulative investigations are required for different solar parks in various climatic zones and architectures. In addition, more experiments about air turbulence and plant processes should be established to figure out the mechanisms causing interactions between microclimate and ecosystem under PV panels. Based on reliable observational data, further study about developing a PV climate model, could help us accurately capture the water and energy exchange processes in the PV farm, for efficient utilization of the PV system.
